profile.name: Tyrolienne (Tyrolienne turque)
profile.tagline: A 1913 piano parody by Erik Satie blending Mozartian themes with waltz-time satire.
profile.insight: Satie’s 'Tyrolienne turque' transforms Mozart’s famous 2/4 Rondo alla turca into a 3/4 time signature, mocking the rigidity of classical forms through deliberate rhythmic distortion.
profile.profile: The 'Tyrolienne turque' is the first movement of Erik Satie’s 1913 piano suite, Croquis et agaceries d'un gros bonhomme en bois. It functions as a musical caricature rather than a documented dance, utilizing parody to subvert classical expectations. The work was premiered by Ricardo Viñes in 1914 and remains a staple of Satie’s humoristic piano repertoire.
profile.profile_long:
The 'Tyrolienne turque' is a singular movement within the piano suite Croquis et agaceries d'un gros bonhomme en bois, composed by Erik Satie between June and August 1913. The suite, whose title translates to 'Sketches and Exasperations of a Big Wooden Dummy,' reflects Satie's penchant for humoristic musical forms and his lifelong antagonism toward the Conservatoire de Paris. The work was published by E. Demets in 1913 and received its public premiere by the pianist Ricardo Viñes at the Salle Pleyel in Paris on March 28, 1914.

Musically, the piece is a deliberate parody. It features a genteel melody that bookends the composition, punctuated by a single 'wrong' note intended to disrupt the decorum of a bourgeois French salon. The core of the piece is a transformation of the famous 'Rondo alla turca' from Mozart’s Piano Sonata No. 11. Satie converts the original 2/4 meter into a 3/4 time signature, effectively stripping the Mozartian theme of its original character. The piece includes an anticipatory bridge passage that Satie instructed the pianist to perform 'With the tips of the eyes.'

While the title suggests a folk dance, the work is strictly a concert piano composition. It is part of a broader trend in Satie's work during this period, which included other humoristic suites such as 'Descriptions automatiques' and 'Embryons desséchés.' The 'gros bonhomme en bois' of the title refers to Satie himself, a self-deprecating moniker he had used since his 1889 performances at Le Chat Noir. The piece has been recorded by numerous pianists throughout the 20th and 21st centuries, including Francis Poulenc, Aldo Ciccolini, and Jean-Yves Thibaudet, cementing its place in the classical piano repertoire as a work of intentional, irreverent satire.

sections.origins_and_history: Composed in 1913 as part of the suite Croquis et agaceries d'un gros bonhomme en bois, the piece was created during a period when Satie was actively producing humoristic piano works. It was premiered in Paris in 1914.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Not a dance; it is a musical composition for piano. No choreography is described in sources.
sections.music_and_instruments: The piece is written for solo piano. It utilizes a 3/4 time signature to parody Mozart's original 2/4 Rondo alla turca.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performed in concert halls or salons, consistent with the classical music tradition of early 20th-century Paris.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The work serves as a musical parody and a critique of classical forms, specifically targeting the rigid structures of the Conservatoire de Paris.
sections.notable_figures: Erik Satie (composer), Ricardo Viñes (pianist who gave the premiere).
sections.lineage: A parody of Mozart's Rondo alla turca.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Parody of 2/4 Rondo alla turca converted to 3/4

claims.text: The suite was composed by Erik Satie in 1913.
claims.quote: Croquis et Agaceries d'un gros bonhomme en bois est un recueil de trois pièces pour piano d'Erik Satie, composé en 1913.

claims.text: The work was premiered by Ricardo Viñes at the Salle Pleyel in 1914.
claims.quote: Ricardo Viñes gave the premiere during a concert of the Société Nationale de Musique at the Salle Pleyel in Paris on March 28, 1914.

claims.text: The 'Tyrolienne turque' is a parody of Mozart's Rondo alla turca.
claims.quote: a parody of the famous rondo alla turca from Mozart's Piano Sonata No. 11 with the theme converted from 24 to 34 time.

claims.text: The title 'gros bonhomme en bois' refers to Satie himself.
claims.quote: The "gros bonhomme en bois" ("Big Wooden Dummy") of the title is the composer himself.

claims.text: The piece includes a specific instruction to be played with the tips of the eyes.
claims.quote: An anticipatory bridge passage (to be played "With the tips of the eyes") leads to the "Turkish yodeling"

claims.text: The first recording of the suite was by Francis Poulenc in 1951.
claims.quote: The Croquis et agaceries d'un gros bonhomme en bois was popular in its day and has been frequently recorded. The first was by Satie's protégé Francis Poulenc in 1951.
